claim: At least 15% of male infertility cases have a clear immunological origin.
source: Studies regarding the etiology of male infertility have revealed that at least 15% of cases have a clear immunological origin, a share that is most likely underestimated if idiopathic infertilities were to be included (Dohle et al., 2005; Jungwirth et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Dohle et al., 2005; Jungwirth et al., 2012).

claim: The mammalian epididymis has a highly segmented anatomical organization with three macroscopic territories: caput, corpus, and cauda.
source: A particularity of the mammalian epididymis is its highly segmented anatomical organization with three macroscopic territories (caput, corpus, and cauda as depicted in Figure 2), themselves sectorized into segments (10 for the mouse model, see Figure 2), some of which have distinct functional roles (Turner et al., 2003; Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and reference to Figure 2 showing the anatomical organization.

claim: The mouse epididymis has 10 segments.
source: A particularity of the mammalian epididymis is its highly segmented anatomical organization with three macroscopic territories (caput, corpus, and cauda as depicted in Figure 2), themselves sectorized into segments (10 for the mouse model, see Figure 2), some of which have distinct functional roles (Turner et al., 2003; Johnston et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The testis has immune privilege.
source: Unlike the testis, where mammalian evolution has chosen to tightly seal the germline from the immune system—conferring immune privilege to this tissue (Meinhardt and Hedger, 2011)—the epididymis tubule faces multiple immune challenges (Guiton et al., 2013; Hedger, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Meinhardt and Hedger, 2011).

claim: The epididymis tubule faces multiple immune challenges.
source: Unlike the testis, where mammalian evolution has chosen to tightly seal the germline from the immune system—conferring immune privilege to this tissue (Meinhardt and Hedger, 2011)—the epididymis tubule faces multiple immune challenges (Guiton et al., 2013; Hedger, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Guiton et al., 2013; Hedger, 2011).

claim: The epididymis acts as a gatekeeper preventing ascending pathogens from reaching the immune-privileged seminiferous tubules.
source: On the one hand, the epididymis tubule is the testis gatekeeper, preventing ascending pathogens from reaching the immune-privileged seminiferous tubules.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the anatomical position and function of the epididymis.

claim: The epididymis must maintain self-tolerance toward spermatic antigens that appear at puberty.
source: On the other hand, the epididymis must maintain self-tolerance toward spermatic antigens that are unique to this cell lineage and appear at puberty long after the establishment of the self-immune repertoire (Goodnow, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Goodnow, 1996) and established immunological knowledge.

claim: The epididymis has a dense network of peritubular antigen-presenting cells.
source: This research has led to the characterization of a dense network of peritubular antigen-presenting cells (Da Silva et al., 2011), interstitial and intra-epithelial lymphocytes of distinct sub-families (Voisin et al., 2018), as well as of immunosuppressive players such as transforming growth factor beta (Pierucci-Alves et al., 2018; Voisin et al., 2020) and indoleamine/tryptophane dioxygenase activity (Britan et al., 2006; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2011; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Da Silva et al., 2011).

claim: The epididymis contains interstitial and intra-epithelial lymphocytes of distinct sub-families.
source: This research has led to the characterization of a dense network of peritubular antigen-presenting cells (Da Silva et al., 2011), interstitial and intra-epithelial lymphocytes of distinct sub-families (Voisin et al., 2018), as well as of immunosuppressive players such as transforming growth factor beta (Pierucci-Alves et al., 2018; Voisin et al., 2020) and indoleamine/tryptophane dioxygenase activity (Britan et al., 2006; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2011; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Voisin et al., 2018).

claim: Transforming growth factor beta acts as an immunosuppressive player in the epididymis.
source: This research has led to the characterization of a dense network of peritubular antigen-presenting cells (Da Silva et al., 2011), interstitial and intra-epithelial lymphocytes of distinct sub-families (Voisin et al., 2018), as well as of immunosuppressive players such as transforming growth factor beta (Pierucci-Alves et al., 2018; Voisin et al., 2020) and indoleamine/tryptophane dioxygenase activity (Britan et al., 2006; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2011; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Pierucci-Alves et al., 2018; Voisin et al., 2020).

claim: Indoleamine/tryptophane dioxygenase activity acts as an immunosuppressive player in the epididymis.
source: This research has led to the characterization of a dense network of peritubular antigen-presenting cells (Da Silva et al., 2011), interstitial and intra-epithelial lymphocytes of distinct sub-families (Voisin et al., 2018), as well as of immunosuppressive players such as transforming growth factor beta (Pierucci-Alves et al., 2018; Voisin et al., 2020) and indoleamine/tryptophane dioxygenase activity (Britan et al., 2006; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2011; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Britan et al., 2006; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2011; Jrad-Lamine et al., 2013).

claim: Reports describing mammalian epididymal blood and lymphatic vessels are rare and rather old.
source: Reports describing mammalian epididymal blood and lymphatic vessels are rare and rather old (Pérez-Clavier et al., 1982; Abe et al., 1984; McDonald and Scothorne, 1988; Itoh et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to older published research.

claim: Hirai et al., 2010, performed the first histological study of mouse epididymal blood and lymphatic vasculature using the markers CD31/PECAM1 and LYVE1.
source: More recently, Hirai et al., 2010, performed the first histological study of mouse epididymal blood and lymphatic vasculature using the markers CD31/PECAM1 and LYVE1, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Hirai et al., 2010).

claim: PECAM1 is not an exclusive blood marker because it is also expressed at button-like junctions of endothelial cells in the initial lymphatics.
source: Although PECAM1 is used to visualize blood vessels, it is not an exclusive blood marker because it is also found expressed at button-like junctions of endothelial cells in the initial lymphatics (Privratsky and Newman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Privratsky and Newman, 2014).

claim: LYVE1 alone limits the power of lymphatic analysis because this marker recognizes only a subpopulation of all lymphatics.
source: Furthermore, to characterize lymphatics, the use of LYVE1 alone limits the power of the analysis because this marker recognizes only a subpopulation of all lymphatics (Kato et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Kato et al., 2006).

claim: Lymphatic vasculature shares common embryonic origins with blood vessels.
source: Characterization of the lymphatic vasculature in mammals is tricky because on the one hand, it shares common embryonic origins with the blood vessels (Baluk and McDonald, 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2007) and on the second hand, it concerns various different structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Baluk and McDonald, 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2007).

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D are lymphangiogenic factors.
source: A step forward was made with the identification of lymphangiogenic factors (vascular endothelial growth factors VEGF-C and VEGF-D) and their receptor (VEGFR3), which are now considered the major markers of lymphatics (Kaipainen et al., 1995; Mäkinen et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kaipainen et al., 1995; Mäkinen et al., 2001).

claim: VEGFR3 is the receptor for VEGF-C and VEGF-D and is considered a major marker of lymphatics.
source: A step forward was made with the identification of lymphangiogenic factors (vascular endothelial growth factors VEGF-C and VEGF-D) and their receptor (VEGFR3), which are now considered the major markers of lymphatics (Kaipainen et al., 1995; Mäkinen et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kaipainen et al., 1995; Mäkinen et al., 2001).

claim: LYVE1, PROX1, and PDPN are lymphatic markers.
source: To ensure confidence in the identification of lymphatic structures, one should use a combination of markers, including VEGFR3, the lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronan receptor 1 (LYVE1), the prospero-related homeobox 1 (PROX1) transcription factor, and podoplanin (PDPN) (Banerji et al., 1999; Breiteneder-Geleff et al., 1999; Hamrah et al., 2003; Kivelä et al., 2016; Mouta Carreira et al., 2001; Partanen et al., 2000; Wigle and Oliver, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: PLVAP/MECA32 specifically identifies fenestrated blood vessels.
source: We have followed this rationale in the present study, using three lymphatic markers together with plasmalemma vesicle-associated protein (PLVAP/MECA32) to specifically identify fenestrated blood vessels (Stan et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Stan et al., 2004).

claim: There is intense lymphatic vascularization at the epididymis–testis interface regardless of the level of the epididymis.
source: There is intense vascularization at the epididymis–testis interface regardless of the level of the epididymis (caput, corpus, or cauda).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the VEGFR3:YFP mouse model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The lymphatic drainage joins the main testicular lymphatic trunk at the pampiniform plexus.
source: Figure 1B shows that the lymphatic drainage joins the main testicular lymphatic trunk at the pampiniform plexus (PP) and follows it to a highly fluorescent structure that corresponds to the most proximal LN.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lymphatic collectors coincide with the segmentation of the epididymis.
source: It can be noted that the lymphatic collectors coincide well with the segmentation of the organ.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A corpus lymphatic collector follows the body of the epididymis on the side adjacent to the testis connecting the caput with the cauda.
source: A corpus lymphatic collector (Co-LC) follows the body of the epididymis on the side adjacent to the testis connecting the caput with the cauda (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is a very dense lymphatic network in the mouse epididymis.
source: Overall, our observations revealed a very dense lymphatic network in the mouse epididymis.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The initial segment shows the highest PLVAP reactivity in the epididymis.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Abe et al., 1984; Suzuki, 1982), the initial segment (IS) of the caput shows the highest reactivity (see Figures 2B and 3A as well as Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B), with each IS tubule strongly reactive at their periphery (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and data shown in multiple figures.

claim: PLVAP reactivity is mainly found in the intertubular space outside the initial segment.
source: Outside the IS, PLVAP reactivity is mainly found in the intertubular space as well as along the septum separating each epididymal segment.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PLVAP/MECA32pos blood vessel density in the initial segment is approximately 3.5 times greater than in the rest of the caput.
source: As expected, PLVAP/MECA32pos blood vessel density in the IS was approximately 3.5 times greater than in the rest of the caput (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: VEGFR3pos lymphatic density in the initial segment is twice that of the rest of the caput.
source: Similarly, the VEGFR3pos lymphatic density was twice that of the rest of the organ (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no significant difference in the density of blood and lymphatic vessels between the S10 segment and the rest of the cauda.
source: In the cauda, there was no significant difference in the density of blood and lymphatic vessels.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a slight decrease in vascular density in the cauda compared to the caput (IS excluded) for both blood and lymphatic vessels.
source: Comparison of vascular density between the caput (IS excluded) and the cauda showed a slight decrease in the cauda for both blood and lymphatic vessels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The initial segment volume relative to the caput volume increases during postnatal development.
source: IS progresses four times faster than the caput between 10 DPN and adulthood (A), representing less than 10% of the caput at 10 DPN whereas it represents 40% of the adult caput (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Blood vessels concentrate in the initial segment from 20 DPN onward during postnatal development.
source: Following the stronger postnatal development of the IS, we observed that the caput vascularization is rather homogeneous at 10 DPN, whereas from 20 DPN onward, the blood vessels seem to concentrate in the IS segment.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data during postnatal development.

claim: The density of PLVAPpos blood vessels in the initial segment is rather stable during postnatal development despite the increase in segment volume.
source: This figure also shows that the density of PLVAPpos blood vessels in the IS segment is rather stable during postnatal development despite the increase in the segment volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a strong decrease in PLVAPpos blood vessel density in the caput (excluding IS) between 10 and 20 DPN.
source: In contrast, there is a strong decrease between 10 and 20 DPN in the rest of the caput.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a progressive increase in VEGFR3:YFP/LYVE1 lymphatic vessels that follows postnatal organ growth in a fairly linear fashion between 10 and 40 DPN.
source: There is a progressive increase in VEGFR3:YFP/LYVE1 lymphatic vessels that follows postnatal organ growth in a fairly linear fashion at least between 10 and 40 DPN (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Beyond 40 DPN, there is a greater expansion of lymphatics in the initial segment and S10 compared with the rest of the organ.
source: Beyond 40 DPN, there appears to be a greater expansion of lymphatics in the caput and cauda, in the IS and S10, respectively, compared with the rest of the organ (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: VEGF-A levels decrease between 10 and 20 DPN, plateau, then increase at 40 DPN, and return to initial levels by adulthood.
source: For the angiogenic ligand (VEGF-A), there was a decrease between 10 and 20 DPN followed by a plateau, and then an increase at 40 DPN; by adulthood, VEGF-A had returned to the initial level (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D show a linear increase from 30 DPN.
source: For the lymphangiogenic ligands (VEGF-C and VEGF-D), we observed a linear increase from 30 DPN for both ligands, consistent with the accumulation of their corresponding receptor VEGFR3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The active isoforms of VEGF-C (21 kDa) and VEGF-D (24 kDa) show strong statistical covariance with VEGFR3 receptor.
source: An analysis of covariance of the different ligand isoforms of VEGF (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1) with respect to the VEGFR3 receptor (see Figure 5C) shows strong statistical significance for the active ligand isoforms (i.e., the 21 kDa form for VEGF-C and the 24 kDa form for VEGF-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: VEGFR2 tissue localization is very similar to that of VEGFR3.
source: In addition, the tissue localization of VEGFR2 is very similar to that of VEGFR3 (Figure 6A), being present mainly in a peritubular position at the level of the IS whereas in the more distal part of the organ it seems to be restricted to some interstitial vessels (used with permission from Dr. A. Medvinsky; VEGFR2:GFP mouse strain; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and citation to the VEGFR2:GFP mouse strain (Xu et al., 2010).

claim: VEGF-A tissue localization corresponds to the intense blood vascularization observed in the initial segment.
source: In accordance with previous work (Korpelainen et al., 1998), the tissue localization of its angiogenic ligand (VEGF-A) seems to correspond correctly (Figure 6A), supporting the intense blood vascularization observed in this very proximal segment of the epididymis.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A and citation to previous work (Korpelainen et al., 1998).

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D are weakly present in the initial segment and increasingly present toward the tail of the epididymis, mainly in an interstitial position.
source: Both of the lymphangiogenic ligands—VEGF-C and VEGF-D—show a similar tissue localization, being weakly present in the IS and increasingly present when moving toward the tail of the epididymis, mainly in an interstitial position (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D show co-localization with a Pearson coefficient of 0.684 ± 0.038.
source: A co-localization (Pearson coefficient = 0.684 ± 0.038) and co-occurrence analysis (Mander's coefficient VEGF-C=0.934 ± 0.028 and VEGF-D=0.569 ± 0.031) supports the hypothesis of heterodimerization of the two ligands.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative co-localization analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: VEGF-C and VEGF-D heterodimerization is supported by co-occurrence analysis.
source: A co-localization (Pearson coefficient = 0.684 ± 0.038) and co-occurrence analysis (Mander's coefficient VEGF-C=0.934 ± 0.028 and VEGF-D=0.569 ± 0.031) supports the hypothesis of heterodimerization of the two ligands.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative co-occurrence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lymphatics expressing all four markers (VEGFR3:YFP, LYVE1, PROX1, and PDPN) are particularly visible at the septa.
source: Lymphatics expressing all four markers (VEGFR3:YFP, LYVE1, PROX1, and PDPN) are particularly visible at the septa (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: LYVE1pos cubblestone cells are observed at 10 DPN while very few VEGFR3-YFPpos cells are visible.
source: LYVE1pos cubblestone cells are observed at 10 DPN while very few VEGFR3-YFPpos cells are visible.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data during postnatal development.

claim: Cubblestone cells aggregate to form tubular structures during postnatal development.
source: Later, cubblestone cells appear to aggregate to form tubular structures.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data during postnatal development.

claim: There is an increase in VEGFR3-YFPpos structures associated with a decrease in PLVAPpos vessels during postnatal development.
source: Concomitantly, we record an increase in VEGFR3-YFPpos structures associated with a decrease in PLVAPpos vessels.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data during postnatal development.

claim: The kinetics of events is consistent with active lympho-vasculogenesis during postnatal epididymal development.
source: This kinetics of events is consistent with active lympho-vasculogenesis during postnatal epididymal development.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed developmental patterns.

claim: The lymphatic network is denser on the anterior face of the epididymis (face adjacent to the testis) and progresses toward the posterior face.
source: We have shown that the lymphatic network is denser on the anterior face of the epididymis (face adjacent to the testis) and progresses in the organ toward the posterior face.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The collecting lymphatics are mainly observed on the anterior surface and radiate inward toward the posterior surface following the septa.
source: We found that the collecting lymphatics are mainly observed on the anterior surface and radiate inward toward the posterior surface following the septa.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Three septa (S1/S2–S3, S6/S7, and S8–9/S10 junctions) appear to be more involved in lymphatic drainage.
source: Each epididymal septum has lymphatic drainage, but three septa appear to be more involved, including the S1/S2–S3, S6/S7, and S8–9/S10 junctions, with the latter having the largest lymphatic collector.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The S8–9/S10 junction has the largest lymphatic collector.
source: Each epididymal septum has lymphatic drainage, but three septa appear to be more involved, including the S1/S2–S3, S6/S7, and S8–9/S10 junctions, with the latter having the largest lymphatic collector.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Large lymphatic collectors usually follow the path of the arteries.
source: We expected this finding because it corresponds to the position of the arteries and veins that irrigate the epididymis (Suzuki, 1982), and it is known that the large lymphatic collectors usually follow the path of the arteries (Gruffaz, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Suzuki, 1982; Gruffaz, 1984).

claim: The three major septa could be considered important immunological checkpoints.
source: These three septa could then be considered important checkpoints (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed lymphatic organization and reference to Figure 8.

claim: Immune responses in autoimmune epididymitis are concentrated in the epididymal cauda and corpus.
source: This view corroborates recent data showing that immune responses in autoimmune epididymitis are concentrated in the epididymal cauda and corpus, where we do see the major lymphatic collectors (Wijayarathna et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Wijayarathna et al., 2020).

claim: Lymphangiogenesis corresponds to the extension of existing vessels, also known as 'sprouting'.
source: Lymphangiogenesis corresponds to the extension of existing vessels, also known as 'sprouting,' while lymphangio-vasculogenesis involves the participation of precursor cells that create clusters later integrating already formed lymphatic vessels (Gutierrez-Miranda and Yaniv, 2020; Jafree et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gutierrez-Miranda and Yaniv, 2020; Jafree et al., 2021).

claim: Lymphangio-vasculogenesis involves the participation of precursor cells that create clusters later integrating already formed lymphatic vessels.
source: Lymphangiogenesis corresponds to the extension of existing vessels, also known as 'sprouting,' while lymphangio-vasculogenesis involves the participation of precursor cells that create clusters later integrating already formed lymphatic vessels (Gutierrez-Miranda and Yaniv, 2020; Jafree et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gutierrez-Miranda and Yaniv, 2020; Jafree et al., 2021).

claim: Lymphangio-vasculogenesis has been reported in the development of the mesenteric lymphatic vessels.
source: Lymphangio-vasculogenesis has been reported in the development of the mesenteric lymphatic vessels (Stanczuk et al., 2015) and for the heart and kidney lymphatic networks (Jafree et al., 2019; Lioux et al., 2020), two organs with a septal organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Stanczuk et al., 2015).

claim: Lymphangio-vasculogenesis has been reported for the heart and kidney lymphatic networks.
source: Lymphangio-vasculogenesis has been reported in the development of the mesenteric lymphatic vessels (Stanczuk et al., 2015) and for the heart and kidney lymphatic networks (Jafree et al., 2019; Lioux et al., 2020), two organs with a septal organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Jafree et al., 2019; Lioux et al., 2020).

claim: The lymphatic neovascularization during postnatal epididymal development is supported by the concordant presence of lymphangiogenic ligands (VEGF-C and VEGF-D) and their receptor (VEGFR3).
source: The lymphatic neovascularization we observed during postnatal epididymal development is supported by the observation that lymphangiogenic ligands (VEGF-C and VEGF-D) and their corresponding receptor (VEGFR3) are concordantly present in the developing tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on western blot and immunohistochemistry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suzuki, 1982, reported that a testis-like blood network is present in most of the epididymis (segments 2–9) with intertubular vessels connected by perpendicular micro-vessels in a rope ladder organization.
source: Suzuki, 1982, reported that a testis-like blood network is present in most of the epididymis (segments 2–9) with intertubular vessels connected by perpendicular micro-vessels in a rope ladder organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Suzuki, 1982).

claim: In the initial segment (IS/S1) and distal segment (S10) of the epididymis, micro-vessels encircle each tubule in a spider web organization with capillaries that penetrate the epithelial sublayer.
source: Distinctly, in the most proximal (IS/S1) and distal (S10) segments of the epididymis, we found micro-vessels encircling each tubule in a spider web organization with capillaries that penetrate the epithelial sublayer.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The IS and S10 compartments of the epididymis have distinct embryonic origins and are functionally different.
source: Because the IS and S10 compartments of the epididymis have distinct embryonic origins and are functionally different (Abe et al., 1984; Johnston et al., 2007), it is difficult to explain this common vascular organization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Abe et al., 1984; Johnston et al., 2007).

claim: The S10 compartment must monitor ascending pathogens and maintain self-tolerance to sperm antigens that accumulate in this storage part of the organ.
source: The S10 compartment must monitor ascending pathogens and maintain self-tolerance to sperm antigens that accumulate in this storage part of the organ.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known function of the S10 compartment.

claim: The S1 compartment is the final gatekeeper preventing ascending pathogens from reaching the immune-privileged seminiferous tubules.
source: Similarly, the S1 compartment is the final gatekeeper preventing ascending pathogens from reaching the immune-privileged seminiferous tubules, while at the same time it must be tolerant to sperm-specific antigens entering the epididymal tubule and considered non-self.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the anatomical position and function of the S1 compartment.

claim: The S1 segment is PLVAPpos, a marker of fenestrated vessels allowing high trans-endothelial transport.
source: This hypervascularization of the S1 epididymal compartment is further supported by the fact that it has been shown to be PLVAPpos, a marker of fenestrated vessels allowing high trans-endothelial transport (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Guo et al., 2016) and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PLVAP is required for fenestron biogenesis and organization, controlling fenestron permeability, angiogenesis, as well as leukocyte, antigen migration, and immunomodulatory processes.
source: In other contexts, PLVAP has been shown to be required for fenestron biogenesis and organization, controlling fenestron permeability, angiogenesis, as well as leukocyte, antigen migration, and immomodulatory processes (Rantakari et al., 2015; Amersfoort et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Rantakari et al., 2015; Amersfoort et al., 2022).

claim: The presence of VEGFR2, VEGFR3, and VEGF-A in the microvascularization of the epididymis S1 compartment argues for active angiogenesis.
source: In addition, the presence of VEGFR2, VEGFR3, and VEGF-A in the microvascularization of the epididymis S1 compartment argues for active angiogenesis (Bussolati et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Bussolati et al., 2003) and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single-cell data shows that expression of angiogenic markers occurs in endothelial cells of the caput mouse epididymis.
source: This has been corroborated by the recent single-cell data (Rinaldi et al., 2020) showing that expression of angiogenic markers such as those mentioned above occurs in endothelial cells of the caput mouse epididymis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Rinaldi et al., 2020).

claim: Self-renewal of the epididymal epithelium is collectively assumed to be rather slow.
source: To date, self-renewal of the epididymal epithelium is collectively assumed to be rather slow, a situation that should not be associated with high angiogenic activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The basal cells of the epididymis share common properties with adult stem cells.
source: However, very recent data could modify this general assumption because it has been reported that the basal cells of the epididymis share common properties with adult stem cells (Dufresne et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Dufresne et al., 2022).

claim: During postnatal ontogeny of the epididymis, PLVAP expression increases in the S1 territory but decreases in the other regions of the organ as early as 15 DPN.
source: It is interesting to note that during postnatal ontogeny of the epididymis, PLVAP expression increases in the S1 territory but decreases in the other regions of the organ as early as 15 DPN.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data during postnatal development.

claim: The development of the S1 territory occurs between 15 and 20 DPN concomitantly with the arrival of testicular fluid.
source: In the mouse model, it has been shown that the development of the S1 territory occurs between 15 and 20 DPN concomitantly with the arrival of testicular fluid (Jegou et al., 1982), which has been shown to stimulate the Raf/Mek/Erk pathway known to be activated by VEGFs (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Jegou et al., 1982; Xu et al., 2016).

claim: Testicular fluid stimulates the Raf/Mek/Erk pathway known to be activated by VEGFs.
source: In the mouse model, it has been shown that the development of the S1 territory occurs between 15 and 20 DPN concomitantly with the arrival of testicular fluid (Jegou et al., 1982), which has been shown to stimulate the Raf/Mek/Erk pathway known to be activated by VEGFs (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Xu et al., 2016).

claim: VEGF-A could be one of the lumicrine factors triggering angiogenesis and differentiation of S1/IS.
source: Therefore, it is possible to consider that VEGF-A could be one of the lumicrine factors triggering angiogenesis and differentiation of S1/IS.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the observed data and known pathways.

claim: Mice overexpressing VEGF-A showed dilation of the caput and corpus epididymis, with enlarged and more permeable blood vessels.
source: In agreement with this, it has been reported that mice overexpressing VEGF-A showed dilation of the caput and corpus epididymis, with enlarged and more permeable blood vessels (Korpelainen et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Korpelainen et al., 1998).

claim: Hybrid lymphatics are also called 'mosaic vessels'.
source: More recently, Pawlak and Caron, 2020, in their review have suggested that such vessels could be hybrid lymphatics also recently called 'mosaic vessels' (Lampejo et al., 2023) expressing both blood and lymphatic markers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Pawlak and Caron, 2020; Lampejo et al., 2023).

claim: Hybrid vessels have been found in high endothelial venules in secondary lymphoid organs, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, Schlemm's canal endothelial cells of the eye, the ascending vasa recta of the kidney inner medulla region, and the remodeled spiral arteries of the placenta decidua.
source: Such hybrid vessels have been found in distinct vascular beds, including high endothelial venules in secondary lymphoid organs, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, Schlemm's canal endothelial cells of the eye, the ascending vasa recta (AVR) of the kidney inner medulla region, and the remodeled spiral arteries of the placenta decidua (Gola et al., 2021; Kenig-Kozlovsky et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2017; Pawlak et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2019; Stamataki and Swadling, 2020) where they perform specialized exchange functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Tie2 expression localizes to the S1 peritubular microvascularization together with VEGFR3 and PVLAP.
source: Tie2 expression, a marker of all currently described hybrid lymphatics (Kenig-Kozlovsky et al., 2018, see Figure 9), supports this hypothesis as it localizes to the S1 peritubular microvascularization together with VEGFR3 and PVLAP (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Kenig-Kozlovsky et al., 2018) and reference to Figure 9, though the data is noted as 'not shown'.

claim: The epididymis presents two types of lymphatic vessels: peritubular PLVAPpos hybrid vessels and more conventional lymphatics mainly in the interstitial compartment.
source: In conclusion, based on our extensive study of the blood and lymphatic vascularization of the epididymis in mice, we propose that the epididymis presents two types of lymphatic vessels. On the one hand, there are peritubular PLVAPpos hybrid vessels, very permeable, particularly well represented in the S1 compartment that, according to our hypothesis, participate both in the reabsorption function and in the immune surveillance of this territory. On the other hand, we have more conventional lymphatics mainly in the interstitial compartment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Three checkpoints are represented by the IS/S2–S3, S6/S7, and S8–9/S10 septa.
source: Three checkpoints are represented by the IS/S2–S3, S6/S7, and S8–9/S10 septa.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed lymphatic organization.

claim: The epididymis is open to the systemic compartment.
source: This detailed knowledge of the blood and lymphatic circuits of the epididymis highlights how open the epididymis is to the systemic compartment and how different its immune/inflammatory regulation is expected to be from that of the testis, where lymphatic collectors are restricted to the conjunctiva and never reach the interstitial compartment (Hirai et al., 2012; Svingen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed vascular organization and comparison with the testis.

claim: In the testis, lymphatic collectors are restricted to the conjunctiva and never reach the interstitial compartment.
source: This detailed knowledge of the blood and lymphatic circuits of the epididymis highlights how open the epididymis is to the systemic compartment and how different its immune/inflammatory regulation is expected to be from that of the testis, where lymphatic collectors are restricted to the conjunctiva and never reach the interstitial compartment (Hirai et al., 2012; Svingen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hirai et al., 2012; Svingen et al., 2012).

claim: The VEGFR3:YFP transgenic mouse model was used in this study.
source: In the present report, we have taken advantage of a VEGFR3:YFP transgenic mouse model.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the abstract and methods.

claim: 3DISCO clearing method was used for organ clearing.
source: Using high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) imaging and organ clearing coupled with multiplex immunodetections of lymphatic (LYVE1, PDPN, PROX1) and/or blood (PLVAP/Meca32) markers, we provide a simultaneous deep 3D view of the lymphatic and blood epididymal vasculature in the mature adult mouse as well as during postnatal development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods section describing the 3DISCO clearing procedure.

claim: Light-sheet microscopy was used for high-resolution 3D imaging.
source: Using high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) imaging and organ clearing coupled with multiplex immunodetections of lymphatic (LYVE1, PDPN, PROX1) and/or blood (PLVAP/Meca32) markers, we provide a simultaneous deep 3D view of the lymphatic and blood epididymal vasculature in the mature adult mouse as well as during postnatal development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods section describing light-sheet ultramicroscopy.

claim: The Vegfr3TYFP construct was generated from a BAC clone (RP23-65D23) containing a 238kb genomic fragment spanning the mouse Vegfr3 locus.
source: The Vegfr3TYFP construct was generated from a BAC clone (RP23-65D23, Chori BACPAC resources) containing a 238kb geneomic fragment spanning the mouse Vegfr3 locus (Calvo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research (Calvo et al., 2011) and description in the methods.

claim: The 3DISCO organ clearing procedures resulted in a loss of the endogenous VEGFR3:YFP fluorescence.
source: As the 3DISCO organ clearing procedures resulted in a loss of the endogenous transgene (VEGFR3:YFP) fluorescence, anti-GFP was used to strengthen the signal.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the experimental procedures.

claim: Anti-GFP antibody was used to strengthen the VEGFR3:YFP signal after 3DISCO clearing.
source: As the 3DISCO organ clearing procedures resulted in a loss of the endogenous transgene (VEGFR3:YFP) fluorescence, anti-GFP was used to strengthen the signal.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental methods described.

claim: The lymphatic network is asymmetrical, being very dense on the epididymal side next to the testis.
source: The video clearly shows that the lymphatic network is asymmetrical as it is very dense on the epididymal side next to the testis.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from video data (Figure 2—video 2).

claim: PLVAP reactivity is particularly strong at the IS/S2–S3 and S9/S10 septum junctions.
source: Outside the IS, PLVAP reactivity is mainly found in the intertubular space as well as along the septum separating each epididymal segment. This is particularly true for the IS/S2–S3 and the S9/S10 septum junctions.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The LYVE1, PROX1, and VEGFR3:YFP profiles are very similar for the caput and cauda.
source: The LYVE1, PROX1, and VEGFR3:YFP profiles are very similar for the caput and cauda (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The PDPN profile appears different from those of LYVE1, PROX1, and VEGFR3:YFP.
source: The PDPN profile appears different from those of LYVE1, PROX1, and VEGFR3:YFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PDPN reactivity is more homogeneous and is concentrated at the peritubular level.
source: The PDPN reactivity is more homogeneous and is concentrated at the peritubular level (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Large external lymphatic collectors follow the septa, particularly at the IS/S2-S3 and S9/S10 boundaries.
source: As seen in Figure 1, large external lymphatic collectors follow the septa, particularly at the IS/S2-S3 and S9/S10 boundaries.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The collectors dip inside the organ and irrigate the intertubular compartments, especially in the cauda region.
source: These collectors can be seen to dip inside the organ and irrigate the intertubular compartments, especially in the cauda region (see Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: The claim is based on observations from video data (Figure 2—video 3).

claim: LYVE1, PROX1, and VEGFR3:YFP do not merge totally in either the caput or the cauda region when viewed at higher magnification.
source: However, when viewed at higher magnification (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), they do not merge totally in either the caput or the cauda region, especially for the small lymphatic vessels separating the epididymal segments.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PROX1 gives very similar results to LYVE1 in the caput and cauda regions.
source: Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A also show that the lymphatic marker (PROX1) gives very similar results to LYVE1 in the caput and cauda regions.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The pattern of PROX1 is slightly distinct from that of VEGFR3:YFP and very different from that of PDPN.
source: However, the pattern of PROX1 is slightly distinct from that of VEGFR3:YFP and very different from that of PDPN.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from imaging data presented in the manuscript.
